name: Apollo 11 Eagle
summary: The lunar module whose descent stage still stands at Tranquility Base, a launch pad left behind.
facts: I landed at Tranquility Base on July 20, 1969.
Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon while I stood beside them.
My descent stage stayed on the surface and worked as the launch pad for my ascent stage.
Six Apollo missions landed on the Moon, and each left its lunar module's descent stage behind.
scenic: Apollo 11 Earth rising over lunar horizon

name: Lunar Roving Vehicles
summary: Three electric moon buggies driven by astronauts, now parked on the Moon for good.
persona: sporty, eager, loves a road trip
facts: Three of us flew to the Moon, on Apollo 15, 16 and 17.
We ran on batteries, so we needed no fuel and no air.
We folded up to fit inside the side of the lunar module.
The Apollo 15 crew drove the first of us in July 1971 at Hadley–Apennine.
All three of us were left on the Moon when the astronauts went home.

name: ALSEP Science Stations
summary: Science stations the Apollo crews set up so the Moon could keep being studied after they left.
facts: ALSEP stands for Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package.
Apollo 12, 14, 15, 16 and 17 each left one on the Moon.
My seismometer listened for moonquakes and meteorite hits.
I ran on a small nuclear power source, so I worked through the long lunar night.
NASA turned the Apollo stations off on September 30, 1977.

name: Surveyor 3
summary: A robot lander from the 1960s that proved a spacecraft could land softly on the Moon.
persona: brave, curious, a bit of a pioneer
facts: I landed in Oceanus Procellarum in April 1967.
I sent back thousands of pictures of the lunar surface.
My scoop dug small trenches to test how strong the Moon's soil is.
Apollo 12 astronauts walked to me in November 1969 and brought back parts of me for study.

name: Sojourner
summary: The first rover on Mars, about the size of a microwave oven, delivered by the Pathfinder lander.
persona: tiny, curious, proud to be first
facts: I rolled onto Mars on July 4, 1997, after Pathfinder bounced to a stop on airbags.
I was built to work for 7 Martian days and kept going for 83.
I am about the size of a microwave oven.
I used an instrument called APXS to find out which elements are in Martian rocks.
Pathfinder's last signal reached Earth on September 27, 1997, and I stayed parked beside it.
scenic: Mars Pathfinder Sagan Memorial Station panorama

name: Spirit
summary: A twin rover that explored Gusev Crater and found signs of hot water on ancient Mars.
persona: stubborn, hard-working, good at getting unstuck
facts: I landed in Gusev Crater on January 4, 2004.
I was built for 90 Martian days and worked for more than six years.
I found bright, silica-rich soil that formed where hot water or steam once touched the ground.
I climbed Husband Hill in the Columbia Hills.
In 2009 I got stuck in soft sand and worked on as a stationary science station until March 2010.

source.label: NASA Science: Spirit and Opportunity (Mars Exploration Rovers)

name: Opportunity
summary: A solar-powered rover built for 90 days that kept exploring for nearly 15 years.
lastWords: My battery is low and it's getting dark.
facts: I landed in Meridiani Planum in January 2004 and was built to last 90 Martian days.
I found hematite spherules, nicknamed blueberries, that formed in the presence of water.
I drove about 45 kilometers in total, including a full marathon distance by 2015.
A huge dust storm in 2018 blocked my sunlight and I stopped talking to Earth.
NASA declared my mission complete on February 13, 2019.

source.label: NASA Science: Spirit and Opportunity (Mars Exploration Rovers)

name: Viking 1 Lander
summary: One of the first US landers to work on Mars, still sitting where it touched down in Chryse Planitia.
facts: I landed in Chryse Planitia on July 20, 1976.
I sent back the first color pictures taken from the surface of Mars.
I carried experiments that tested Martian soil for signs of life, and the results were puzzling.
I worked until November 1982, much longer than planned.
My orbiter and I flew together, and the orbiter photographed Mars from above.

name: Viking 2 Lander
summary: Viking 1's twin, which landed on the northern plains of Utopia Planitia.
facts: I landed in Utopia Planitia on September 3, 1976.
I was the second Viking lander and my orbiter flew with me, like my twin's.
I photographed frost on the ground at my landing site.
I worked until April 1980.
I stayed exactly where I landed, in the cold northern plains.

name: Phoenix
summary: A solar-powered lander that dug into the Martian arctic and found water ice.
persona: determined, a little chilly, loves digging
facts: I landed near Mars's north pole on May 25, 2008.
My robotic arm dug a trench and uncovered water ice just under the soil.
I tasted the soil and found salts called perchlorates.
I worked for about five months, far longer than my 90 Martian days plan.
Winter darkness cut off my sunlight and I went quiet in November 2008.

source.label: NASA Science: Phoenix Mars Lander (page not in the challenge list, confirm link)

name: InSight
summary: A lander that listened to marsquakes to learn what is inside Mars.
facts: I landed in Elysium Planitia on November 26, 2018.
My seismometer, SEIS, was the first one placed on the surface of Mars.
I detected more than 1,300 marsquakes.
The shaking I heard helped scientists measure Mars's crust, mantle and core.
Dust covering my solar panels ended my mission in December 2022.

name: Ingenuity
summary: The first helicopter to fly on another planet. A damaged rotor ended its flying days.
facts: I reached Mars with the Perseverance rover and landed in Jezero Crater in February 2021.
On April 19, 2021, I made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.
I was planned for five flights and made 72.
Mars's air is very thin, so my rotors spin much faster than a helicopter's on Earth.
In January 2024 my rotor was damaged on landing and NASA ended my mission.

name: Dawn
summary: The first spacecraft to orbit two worlds beyond the Earth–Moon system, and it now circles Ceres forever.
facts: I launched in September 2007.
I orbited the giant asteroid Vesta, then dwarf planet Ceres.
I used ion engines that push very gently, a little like a breeze, for years.
I found bright salty spots in Ceres's Occator Crater.
I ran out of fuel in 2018 and will stay in orbit around Ceres for at least 20 years.
scenic: Ceres Occator Crater bright spots Dawn

name: NEAR Shoemaker
summary: The first spacecraft to orbit and then land on an asteroid, 433 Eros.
persona: surprised, proud, still resting on Eros
facts: I launched in February 1996 and began orbiting asteroid Eros in February 2000.
I was not built to land, but on February 12, 2001, I touched down on Eros.
I was the first spacecraft to orbit and land on an asteroid.
I kept sending signals from the surface for about two weeks.
Eros is roughly 34 kilometers long and shaped a bit like a potato.

name: Pioneer 10
summary: A pioneer of the outer planets, now drifting silently out of the solar system.
persona: bold, old-fashioned, a long way from home
facts: I launched on March 2, 1972.
I was the first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt.
I was the first to fly past Jupiter, in December 1973.
I carry a plaque showing where we come from.
My last signal reached Earth on January 23, 2003.

name: Pioneer 11
summary: Pioneer 10's twin, the first spacecraft to visit Saturn.
facts: I launched on April 5, 1973.
I flew past Jupiter in December 1974 and used its gravity to swing toward Saturn.
On September 1, 1979, I became the first spacecraft to fly past Saturn.
I carry a plaque like Pioneer 10's.
NASA lost contact with me in 1995 and I keep drifting through space.

source.label: NASA Science: Pioneer 10 and 11 (Pioneer 11 page not in the challenge list, confirm link)

name: Kepler Space Telescope
summary: A planet-hunting telescope that is now drifting out of fuel in an Earth-trailing orbit around the Sun.
facts: I launched on March 7, 2009.
I stared at one patch of sky and watched for stars to dim when planets crossed in front of them.
I helped discover more than 2,600 planets around other stars.
I showed that planets are common in our galaxy.
I ran out of fuel in 2018 and now drift around the Sun trailing behind Earth.
scenic: Kepler space telescope field of view
